item.text: {"candidates":[{"draft_id":"D0061","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Current administration flagship reforms include USMCA implementation, minimum wage increases, subcontracting law to reduce wage inequality, increased social pension, and Isthmus of Tehuantepec trade corridor development.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican administration (AMLO)","action":"implementing USMCA; increasing minimum wage; enacting subcontracting law; increasing general social pension; developing Isthmus of Tehuantepec corridor","mechanism":null,"outcome":"Policy agenda focused on redistribution, trade promotion, infrastructure investment, and trade integration, especially for Southern states","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Flagship reforms include (i) the implementation of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA); (ii) increases in the minimum wage and the subcontracting law to reduce wage inequality; (iii) increases in the general social pension to reduce old age poverty; and (iv) the development of trade infrastructure in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec.","locator":"page 28","attribution":"IMF Country Report","period_fit":"AMLO administration through 2022","source_limitations":["Staff characterization of administration policies"],"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.4","5B.8"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verbatim from page 28 para 46. Claim matches excerpt closely; 'increased social pension' is acceptable shorthand for 'increases in the general social pension to reduce old age poverty'. Action field correctly inferred from excerpt."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0062","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"IMF staff recommended gradual increase in productive government spending of 2-3% of GDP financed by revenue-raising tax reforms to foster inclusive growth and address pandemic legacies.","claim_type":"recommendation","polarity":"favorable","actor":"IMF staff","action":null,"mechanism":null,"outcome":"Recommended: 2-4% GDP increase in productive spending on education, health, public investment, and social safety nets to achieve SDG progress","dates":[],"quantities":["2-4% of GDP recommended spending increase"],"excerpt":"A gradual, permanent increase in spending of around 2 to 3 percent of GDP could foster inclusive growth, reduce poverty, and address pandemic legacies. This feasible step would help make progress in achieving the Social Development Goals.","locator":"page 28","attribution":"IMF staff","period_fit":"IMF 2022 recommendations","source_limitations":["Recommendation, not enacted policy"],"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.6","5B.8","5B.10"],"verification_status":"corrected","verification_notes":["Outcome modified: excerpt states 'help make progress in achieving the Social Development Goals.' Claim matches excerpt exactly. Additional outcome context about pandemic and education spending needs is supported by the surrounding paragraph ('The pandemic has further increased spending needs, particularly in education (following 18 months of school closures)')."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0064","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"IMF staff proposed comprehensive tax reforms including VAT rationalization, personal income tax base expansion, subnational property tax increases, and carbon tax raising to USD 75/ton by 2030.","claim_type":"recommendation","polarity":"mixed","actor":"IMF staff","action":null,"mechanism":null,"outcome":"Recommended reforms: eliminate most zero-ratings and exemptions on VAT; eliminate PIT exclusions; widen top PIT bracket (yield ~0.75% GDP); property tax increase (~0.75% GDP); carbon tax to USD 75/ton by 2030 (yield ~1.8% GDP by 2030)","dates":[],"quantities":["~0.75% GDP from PIT reforms","~0.75% GDP from property taxes","~1.8% GDP by 2030 from carbon tax","USD 75/ton carbon tax by 2030 (from USD 3/ton current)"],"excerpt":"A comprehensive risk management strategy and a high-coverage audit process for VAT returns could also reduce the compliance gap. Eliminating exclusions, reducing tax expenditure, and widening the top personal income tax bracket. These measures could yield around ¾ percent of GDP. Property taxes could be increased gradually to raise over ¾ percent of GDP. The carbon tax remains relatively narrow in scope... the tax rate (USD 3 per ton of CO2) is very low and should be raised to USD 75 by 2030.","locator":"page 29","attribution":"IMF staff","period_fit":"IMF 2022 recommendations with projected 2030 timeline","source_limitations":["Recommendations not enacted; carbon price projections subject to assumptions"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.8"],"verification_status":"corrected","verification_notes":["Quantities array and outcome corrected: the ~1.8% GDP figure comes from 'such a carbon price, combined with an expansion of emissions pricing coverage' (not carbon tax alone), per Black and others 2021. Candidate incorrectly attributes 1.8% to carbon tax alone. Also omits: (1) 'along the lines of the global carbon tax floor proposed for G20 economies'; (2) 'a compensation scheme would be needed for those most negatively affected.' These omissions affect the completeness of the recommendation framing."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0065","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's non-oil revenue was nearly 6% of GDP below Latin American peers and about half the OECD average before the pandemic.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexican government revenue system","action":null,"mechanism":null,"outcome":"Significant tax revenue gap relative to regional and OECD peers; tax administration strengthening underway but policy reforms also needed","dates":["pre-pandemic baseline"],"quantities":["nearly 6% of GDP below Latin American peers","about half the OECD average (non-oil revenue)"],"excerpt":"Mexico's non-oil revenue was nearly 6 percent of GDP below Latin American peers (and only about half the OECD average) before the pandemic.","locator":"page 29","attribution":"IMF staff analysis","period_fit":"Pre-pandemic baseline (2019)","source_limitations":[],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.10"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verbatim from page 29 para 50. Claim matches exactly including 'nearly 6 percent' and 'about half the OECD average.' Dates correctly identified as pre-pandemic baseline."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0066","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Pemex restructuring needs to continue: focus on production in profitable fields, sell non-core assets, reform pension scheme, and increase private partnerships in upstream projects.","claim_type":"recommendation","polarity":"context","actor":"Pemex / Mexican government","action":null,"mechanism":null,"outcome":"Recommended: focus on profitable fields; sell non-core assets; reform pension scheme; more private partnerships in upstream to maintain/increase production at lower cost and reduce fiscal risks","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Changes to the business plan should remain a priority, including focusing on production in profitable fields, selling non-core assets, and reforming its pension scheme. Claim correctly characterizes restructuring recommendations. 'More partnerships with private firms in upstream' correctly paraphrased from 'More partnerships with private firms in upstream projects.'"],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0067","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Fiscal gap estimated at 0.2% of GDP in 2023, gradually increasing to ~1.3% by 2027 absent policy changes; authorities have closed gaps through measures and small deficit target changes.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexican government","action":null,"mechanism":null,"outcome":"Medium-term fiscal gap requiring policy response; authorities addressed through revenue/spending measures and deficit target adjustments","dates":["2023-2027 projection period"],"quantities":["0.2% of GDP gap in 2023","~1.3% of GDP by 2027"],"excerpt":"Based on staff's macroeconomic forecasts, there is a fiscal gap of 0.2 percent of GDP in 2023, which gradually increases to around 1.3 percent of GDP by 2027. Period fit appropriate."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0069","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Contract enforcement by civil justice is very weak in Mexico, discouraging business expansion, formal employment, collateral seizure, and financial development.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexican civil justice system","action":null,"mechanism":null,"outcome":"Weak contract enforcement undermines business expansion, formal employment, collateral seizure, and financial development","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Contract enforcement by civil justice is very weak, discouraging business expansion and formal employment. Attribution to 'IMF Country Report' is accurate."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0070","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"IMF recommended implementing anti-corruption framework including treating corruption and fraud as felony offenses, whistleblower protection, empowering investigation/prosecution/oversight institutions, and participating in voluntary transnational corruption assessments.","claim_type":"recommendation","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican government","action":null,"mechanism":null,"outcome":"New law treating corruption/fraud as felony offenses expected to enable more comprehensive investigations; challenge lies in implementation and effectiveness assessment","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"A new law treating corruption and fraud as felony offenses is expected to enable more comprehensive investigations on corruption. Prevention, facilitation of reporting including with whistleblowing protection and further empowering the institutions in charge of investigation, prosecution and oversight can improve implementation.","locator":"page 30","attribution":"IMF staff","period_fit":"IMF 2022 assessment","source_limitations":["Law passed/pending; implementation and effectiveness not yet demonstrated"],"question_ids":["5B.5","5B.7"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt accurately reflects page 30 para 53. The phrase 'treating corruption and fraud as felony offenses' matches source. Whistleblowing protection and institution-empowerment are correctly extracted. Attribution to IMF staff is accurate."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0071","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexican authorities support pro-growth productive spending increase and tax reforms but note implementation requires time; they expressed confidence in administrative measures to combat tax evasion and fraud.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexican authorities","action":null,"mechanism":"administrative measures to combat tax evasion and tax fraud","outcome":"Authorities supportive of reform direction but emphasize time requirements; confident in continued robust revenues from anti-evasion/fraud administration","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"They are supportive of a pro-growth productive spending increase supported by tax reforms. Actor correctly identified as Mexican authorities. mechanism correctly extracted. Attribution to authorities' views is accurate and appropriately labeled as their position vs. IMF staff recommendation."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0072","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"IMF staff recommended mortgage market macroprudential regulation: introduce loan-to-value and debt-to-income requirements early given rapid growth, publish macroprudential strategy and counter-cyclical buffer guidelines.","claim_type":"recommendation","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican authorities / Banxico / CNBV","action":null,"mechanism":null,"outcome":"Recommended: loan-to-value and debt-to-income requirements for mortgage market; macroprudential strategy publication; counter-cyclical buffer guidelines","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Introducing loan-to-value and debt-to-income requirements at this early stage would be prudent, ahead of a possible risk build-up. Candidate correctly paraphrases the recommendation. Actor field adds 'Banxico / CNBV' which are not in this specific excerpt but are appropriate given context (Banxico = Bank of Mexico, CNBV = banking regulator, both mentioned in surrounding paragraphs). Attribution to IMF staff is accurate. Minor correction: the excerpt says 'at this early stage' not 'given rapid growth' — however 'ahead of a possible risk build-up' conveys the same prudential rationale."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0073","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The 2021 pension reform reduced qualifying weeks for pension eligibility and raised contribution rates.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexico federal government","action":"enacted pension reform","mechanism":"reduced qualifying weeks for pension eligibility; raised contribution rates","outcome":"reduced formal labor supply incentives","dates":["2021"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"The 2021 pension reform risks reducing formal labor supply incentives, including by reducing the number of qualifying weeks for pension eligibility and raising contribution rates.","locator":"page 31","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, Article IV Consultation, MAC-010","period_fit":"2021 reform in effect during assessment period; risk identified by IMF staff","source_limitations":["IMF staff analytical assessment rather than confirmed outcome; policy effect on formal labor supply is characterized as a risk"],"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.8"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt accurately reflects page 31 para 54. The claim 'reduced qualifying weeks and raised contribution rates' correctly describes the policy actions. The source characterizes the effect as a 'risk' — candidate's outcome 'reduced formal labor supply incentives' appropriately captures this as an identified risk rather than a confirmed outcome. Source limitations correctly note this is an analytical risk assessment."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0074","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Minimum wage increases of 50.4 percent cumulative were projected for 2023-2024, raising informality risk and reducing opportunities for formal sector transition.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexico federal government","action":"raised minimum wages substantially","mechanism":"cumulative real minimum wage increases of approximately 50.4 percent through 2024","outcome":"increased informality risk; reduced formal sector transition opportunities; risks offsetting formalization gains","dates":["2023","2024"],"quantities":["50.4 percent cumulative minimum wage growth (2023-2024 est.)"],"excerpt":"Recent reforms to reduce inequality—notably increases in the minimum wage—risk increasing incentives for informality and reduce opportunities for workers to transition to the formal sector.","locator":"page 31","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, Article IV Consultation, MAC-010","period_fit":"2023-2024 policy period; directly relevant to economic distribution and formalization trajectory","source_limitations":["IMF staff analytical risk assessment; minimum wage policy is an observed policy action with staff-characterized risks rather than confirmed outcomes"],"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.8"],"verification_status":"corrected","verification_notes":["Claim corrected: The 50.4 percent figure appears in the footnote chart caption ('Minimum wages for 2023 and 2024 are estimated based on assumption of 50.4 percent cumulative growth') and describes a projected/estimated increase, not an already-enacted cumulative total. The excerpt used for the main claim does not mention the 50.4 percent figure. The 50.4 percent is in the footnote to the chart on page 31, not in para 54 itself. Attribution to para 54 excerpt is therefore partially unsupported by that specific excerpt. The 50.4% should be attributed to the footnote/chart caption, not to para 54. Dates array ['2023','2024'] is correct as projections. Source limitations appropriately characterize this as staff risk assessment."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0075","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The USMCA trade agreement was implemented with independent labor adjudication courts established at the state level under the 2019 labor law, accelerating labor dispute resolution.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexico federal government; U.S. and Canadian governments","action":"implemented USMCA; established independent labor adjudication courts at state level","mechanism":"bilateral trade agreement reducing regulatory divergence and eliminating tariffs; state-level independent labor courts under 2019 labor law","outcome":"accelerated resolution of labor disputes; compliance with USMCA labor provisions","dates":["2019","2022"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"The agreement with the U.S. and Canada reduces regulatory divergence, complementing the elimination of many tariffs under NAFTA. Implementation efforts include the establishment of new, independent labor adjudication courts at the state level.","locator":"page 32","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, Article IV Consultation, MAC-010","period_fit":"2019 law implementation ongoing through 2022; USMCA in effect","source_limitations":["Staff characterization of acceleration; no independent verification of court capacity or throughput cited"],"question_ids":["5B.4","5B.7"],"verification_status":"corrected","verification_notes":["Outcome corrected: 'accelerated resolution of labor disputes' — the cited excerpt (page 32 para 55) does not state this. That claim appears in the Authorities' Views section (page 33 para 58): 'The authorities were pleased that the implementation of the 2019 labor law had already resulted in accelerated resolution of labor disputes.' The candidate has cross-sourced from a different page, and the acceleration claim is the authorities' self-report, not IMF staff characterization. Excerpt itself is from para 55 but the acceleration claim belongs to para 58."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0076","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's autonomous competition authority experienced budget cuts and its statutory independence was impaired, reducing its capacity to enforce competition rules.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexico competition authority (COFECE and/or IFT)","action":"experienced budget cuts; faced threats to statutory independence","mechanism":"budget reductions; recent legislative or executive actions threatening independence","outcome":"weakened competition enforcement; reduced ability to counteract firm concentration and barriers to entry","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"The autonomous competition authority should be strengthened by reversing recent budget cuts and preserving its statutory independence.","locator":"page 32","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, Article IV Consultation, MAC-010","period_fit":"Assessment period 2022; ongoing institutional degradation","source_limitations":["Staff recommendation rather than confirmed outcome; specific budget cut amounts and independence threats not detailed in this passage"],"question_ids":["5B.5"],"verification_status":"rejected","verification_notes":["Rejected: The cited excerpt (page 32, end of para 55) is entirely a forward-looking recommendation ('should be strengthened by reversing...and preserving'). It does not state or assert that cuts have already occurred or that independence has already been impaired. The candidate presents a should-statement as an observed fact. The source describes what the IMF believes should happen (strengthening), not what has happened (cuts and impairment). claim_type should be 'recommendation' not 'source_assertion', and the claim itself is unsupported by this excerpt. A separate passage confirming actual budget cuts would be needed to support this as a source_assertion."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0077","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Foreign direct investment restrictions in surface, maritime, and air transport limit competition; cumbersome licensing and permits create corruption vulnerabilities.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexico federal government","action":"maintained FDI restrictions in transport sectors; maintained cumbersome licensing and permit procedures","mechanism":"FDI restrictions in surface, maritime, and air transport; licensing and permit procedures in road transport, custom brokerage, restaurants, and construction","outcome":"limited competition in transport sectors; corruption vulnerabilities in regulated activities","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Regulatory hurdles in some sectors with critical forward linkages (e.g., foreign direct investment restrictions in surface, maritime and air transport) limit competition and, through the implications for input costs, harms the competitiveness of other sectors. Also, cumbersome licenses and permits procedures create vulnerabilities to corruption (e.g., road transport, custom brokerage and restaurants licenses, construction permits).","locator":"page 32","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, Article IV Consultation, MAC-010","period_fit":"Assessment period 2022; persistent structural barriers","source_limitations":["Staff characterization of sector-level effects; specific affected sectors cited as examples rather than exhaustive enumeration"],"question_ids":["5B.4","5B.5"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verbatim from page 32 para 55. FDI restrictions in surface/maritime/air transport and cumbersome licensing in road transport, custom brokerage, restaurants, and construction all match source. Candidate adds 'maintained' implying ongoing policy — acceptable inference from the continuous-tense source language. Source limitations about sector examples are appropriate."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0078","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico reversed key elements of the 2013 energy reform: a new electricity law replaced market auctions with non-market policies, concentrated regulatory power in CFE, disrupted existing contracts, and created conflicts of interest.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexico federal government; Parliament (Congress)","action":"enacted new electricity law replacing 2013 reform; rejected full constitutional reversal of 2013 reform","mechanism":"Parliament-approved new electricity law with non-market policies; regulatory power concentrated in CFE; contracts from 2013 reform disrupted","outcome":"policy uncertainty about energy sector direction; conflicts of interest; disrupted private contracts; reduced private sector participation in energy","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Actions to reverse the 2013 energy reforms remain incomplete, as Parliament rejected the change in the constitution needed for a full reversal, which has introduced policy uncertainty about the way forward. A new electricity law, however, was approved and has replaced auctions by nonmarket-based policies, with regulatory power given to the Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE), the state-owned electricity company. This has created conflicts of interest and disrupted contracts signed under the 2013 reform.","locator":"page 33","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, Article IV Consultation, MAC-010","period_fit":"Post-2013 reform period; new law enacted prior to 2022 assessment; incomplete reversal and new law represent ongoing policy uncertainty","source_limitations":["Staff characterization of policy effects; contracts disrupted and conflicts of interest are staff assertions without quantified extent"],"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.3","5B.4","5B.9"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verbatim from page 33 para 56. All key elements verified: 'reversed key elements' (partial reversal via new electricity law), 'replaced auctions by nonmarket-based policies,' 'regulatory power given to CFE,' 'created conflicts of interest,' 'disrupted contracts.' Actor correctly identifies both federal government and Parliament. The note about Parliament rejecting constitutional change (incomplete reversal) is accurate."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0079","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's 2023 emission trading system pilot covers approximately 40 percent of emissions from a limited number of large entities, with no legally binding emissions caps and unclear scalability.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexico federal government","action":"expanded ETS in 2023 to pilot phase","mechanism":"pilot emission trading system covering large entities responsible for approximately 40 percent of emissions; auction system for allowances not yet introduced; no legally binding caps","outcome":"ETS market remains limited; ability to expand coverage is not clear; legally binding caps absent","dates":["2023"],"quantities":["approximately 40 percent of emissions covered (pilot phase)"],"excerpt":"Although these are responsible for around 40 percent of emissions, the ability to expand coverage is not clear. Additionally, the size of the allocated allowances and the absence of legally binding emissions caps mean that the market created by the pilot is limited.","locator":"page 33","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, Article IV Consultation, MAC-010","period_fit":"2023 ETS expansion in pilot phase; coverage and enforcement limitations as of assessment date","source_limitations":["Staff characterization of coverage; no independent verification of actual emissions coverage percentage; scalability questions are staff assessments of uncertainty rather than confirmed barriers"],"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.3"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt accurately reflects page 33 para 57. The 'approximately 40 percent' matches 'around 40 percent.' 'No legally binding emissions caps' matches 'absence of legally binding emissions caps.' 'Unclear scalability' matches 'ability to expand coverage is not clear.' The surrounding context (not in excerpt) confirms this is a 2023 expansion. Source limitations are appropriate."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0080","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's authorities prioritized increased public investment in underdeveloped areas and industrial policy to reduce regional disparities and build human capital, while supporting energy state-owned enterprises.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexico federal government (authorities)","action":"increased public investment in underdeveloped areas; prioritized industrial policy and human capital; strengthened energy state-owned enterprises","mechanism":"public investment targeting underdeveloped regions; industrial policy and human capital investment; regulatory framework strengthening CFE and Pemex","outcome":"intended support for growth and regional disparity reduction; authorities' stated approach to productivity improvement","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"The authorities pointed to a sharp increase in public investment especially in underdeveloped areas, to support growth and reduce regional disparities. They considered industrial policy and strengthening human capital as major priorities to increase productivity. The authorities were seeking to increase labor market formality with the outsourcing law and tax administration reforms. They considered that a regulatory framework strengthening their energy state-owned enterprises served the economy better.","locator":"page 33","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, Article IV Consultation, MAC-010","period_fit":"Lopez Obrador administration priorities; 2018-2022 assessment period","source_limitations":["Authorities' self-reported claims; staff does not independently verify magnitude or effectiveness of investment; energy state-owned enterprise strengthening contradicts IMF market-oriented recommendations (divergent assessment)"],"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.6","5B.8","5B.10"],"verification_status":"corrected","verification_notes":["Outcome corrected: The source text (para 58, Authorities' Views) presents what authorities pointed to and considered as priorities — this is their self-reported position, not a confirmed outcome or an IMF-endorsed assessment. Candidate's outcome 'intended support for growth and regional disparity reduction' attributes intended outcomes as though they are confirmed, when they are authorities' stated aims. The source limitations field is appropriate and captures the self-reporting nature. The polarity 'favorable' is also questionable given the source itself notes this approach 'contradicts IMF market-oriented recommendations' — a more accurate polarity might be 'mixed' or the source limitations should be elevated to a polarity note."],"premium_verification_required":false}],"material_omissions":[],"unresolved_gaps":[]}
